I am 55 years old and have farmed this land in Quzhou County for 40 years. My husband and I manage these 18 mu together, and our son works off-farm in the county town, so it is mostly the two of us in the fields. We have a wheat-maize rotation — this is the only system I know, and it has fed our family well for decades.

Since it is the start of the growing season, the winter wheat I sowed last October is just beginning to green up. I will apply a top-dressing of urea at green-up to help the wheat tiller well, and then irrigate from our well because the spring drought on the North China Plain is severe. I will irrigate again at jointing and once more at grain filling. For the wheat, I always use improved varieties — the seeds from the county supply store — because they yield better and resist lodging. I till with the rotary tiller before sowing in autumn, but now in spring I only need to manage the standing crop. I will spray pesticides twice if I see aphids or powdery mildew, which is common here. I expect about 500 kg per mu from the wheat if the weather cooperates.

After the wheat harvest in early June, there is no time to waste. I will immediately rotary-till the stubble and plant hybrid maize the same day — every day of delay costs yield. The maize will get basal fertilizer at sowing and a side-dressing of nitrogen at the big-flare stage. I will irrigate twice: once if the June dry spell hits, and again at flowering to ensure the kernels fill properly. I will spray herbicide once and insecticide once or twice depending on armyworm pressure. With our well and the summer heat, I expect about 550 kg per mu from the maize.

We cannot afford to spare any land — all 18 mu go to wheat in winter and maize in summer. This is what we have always done, and with only two of us farming, keeping the plot size manageable but fully utilized is the only way to make ends meet.
